Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give a quick run through the quality metrics then dig into the edge cases. um arjun and i will cover the scoring updates.
[00:22] Arjun Patel: hi all, quick note my screen's shared i think? lmk if you can't see the scoring sheet, i've highlighted the new columns -- confidence bands and hallucination flags.
[00:40] Sara Lopez: yep seeing it, thanks. quick context: we've been running the model on the 1k prompt set and saw a spike in hallucination on rare medication names, also some drop on instruction-following.
[01:05] Tom Nguyen: right and recalling our success criteria is <2% hallucination on clinical entities and >=92% instruction adherence across top use cases.
[01:22] Arjun Patel: correct, those are the targets we baked into the rubric. so the latest run on the redwood-hosted variant (v0.9-quant) shows 3.8% hallucination on rare meds and 89% instruction adhesion -- uh adherence, my bad.
[01:45] Priya Singh: yeah we noticed the rare tokens, specifically brand names that are less frequent in public corpora, the model sometimes invents dosing.
[02:10] Maya Chen: okay let's walk through the concrete examples. arjun, can you show one or two transcripts where the model hallucinates a dose?
[02:25] Arjun Patel: sure — example timestamp 00:12 in the sheet: prompt about prescribing to elderly patient, model suggests "200 mg twice daily" for a med that is usually in micrograms. it's clearly a scale error.
[02:48] Sara Lopez: that's the one, and it's reproducible with similar prompts. we added paraphrases to the prompt set but it still shows up.
[03:10] Arjun Patel: we dug in — looks like tokenization + quantization might push probabilities for numeric sequences. when we ran the FP16 variant hallucination dropped to 2.1% but latency increased ~45ms per request.
[03:35] Tom Nguyen: tradeoff question: can we accept slightly higher latency for better safety? ops cost wise is that a big hit?
[03:50] Maya Chen: good question, costs rise but the Optimize suggestions show batching and prefix cache could recoup some tokens, and Dedicated reserved capacity would control unit costs. we'll share estimates.
[04:10] Priya Singh: from compliance side, hallucination on meds is non-negotiable; we need a strict guardrail and fallback path to safe responses.
[04:27] Arjun Patel: agreed. we recommended a two-layer guardrail: 1) model-side prompting + constrained decoding to reduce invented numeric tokens and 2) post-hoc rule-based verifier for numeric ranges that triggers a safe fallback or ask-for-clarification response.
[04:50] Sara Lopez: what's the false positive rate on the rule verifier? we don't want it to degrade UX by overblocking.
[05:05] Arjun Patel: in our internal checks the rule-based verifier catches 92% of out-of-range numeric hallucinations and false positives are about 3-4% on benign cases; we can tune thresholds per workload.
[05:30] Maya Chen: note we've added a scoring column 'regression_alert' which sets off when current run deviates >1.5 std from baseline on any metric. the March 1 baseline was used here.
[05:52] Sara Lopez: and that triggered for hallucination on March 2 run?
[06:00] Arjun Patel: yes exactly, hence the alert. we also track prompt-level scores so we can identify top 20 failing prompts.
[06:15] Priya Singh: can we get the top 20 failing prompts exported with paraphrases? that would help us craft guardrail rules.
[06:28] Maya Chen: yes we'll export them. arjun will include paraphrases where we've seen the failure.
[06:40] Tom Nguyen: another item—what about model variants? you mentioned v0.9-quant vs FP16. is there a middle ground like q4_0 that keeps safety without big latency hit?
[06:55] Arjun Patel: we tested q4_0 and saw hallucination at ~2.6% and latency only +20ms. it's promising as a compromise. also can route critical prompts to FP16 and regular to q4_0 via smart routing.
[07:20] Sara Lopez: routing adds complexity to infra, but it's ok if you provide a config we can plug into our gateway.
[07:33] Maya Chen: we can provide a routing policy example and a canary rollout plan so you can validate on a small percentage first.
[07:45] Priya Singh: about guardrails — can you show an example prompt template that reduces hallucination?
[07:54] Arjun Patel: sure, current recipe is: system message that sets constraints, explicit numeric formatting instruction, and a final safety check prompt instructing the model to verify any numeric recommendation before returning. example: "If recommending dosages, confirm units and ranges; if uncertain, respond 'insufficient info' and ask for clarification."
[08:20] Sara Lopez: hmm, that seems helpful. does that affect instruction adherence metrics?
[08:28] Arjun Patel: slightly — instruction adherence improved for safety but some instructions requiring generative elaboration saw a tiny dip. it's a balance.
[08:40] Maya Chen: moving to regression checks — we've implemented eval hooks that re-run a fixed eval set daily and alert when drift exceeds thresholds. here's a screenshot of the dashboard.
[09:00] Tom Nguyen: what alerting channels do you support? we want pager duty for sev1 regressions and slack for warnings.
[09:08] Arjun Patel: pagerduty, slack, email, webhook. you can map alert severity to channels.
[09:18] Priya Singh: will the alerts include prompt examples and diffs? that would speed triage.
[09:24] Arjun Patel: yes, we include the top diffs and sample inputs/outputs in the alert payload, and a link to the dashboard with the full context.
[09:36] Sara Lopez: can you also include model metadata (variant, quant, kernel selection) in the alert?
[09:42] Arjun Patel: absolutely, kernel+quantization+hardware are included in the alert.
[09:50] Maya Chen: quick pause — any legal/compliance notes?
[09:54] Tom Nguyen: we need encryption at rest and in transit, KMS integration, and audit logs for PHI access. also SOC2 report and data residency info.
[10:06] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports customer KMS and audit logs; we can share SOC2 and the compliance pack. action: maya will share the security docs.
[10:18] Sara Lopez: thanks.
[10:22] Arjun Patel: going back to scoring, we added a metric 'semantic drift' measured via embedding distance to baseline answers, it caught the instruction-following drop.
[10:36] Priya Singh: interesting, embedding drift is useful. can that be tuned to downweight common synonyms?
[10:43] Arjun Patel: yes, the drift threshold is configurable per intent cluster; we can group prompts and tune sensitivity.
[10:52] Maya Chen: next, let's review the proposed pilot timeline: collect extra prompts this week, run a full benchmark (latency+throughput+safety) next Wed, then review. everyone ok?
[11:06] Sara Lopez: yes that works for us.
[11:10] Tom Nguyen: fine.
[11:12] Priya Singh: ok.
[11:15] Arjun Patel: final Q: for the benchmark, what load profile do you want? production-like bursty traffic or steady?
[11:23] Tom Nguyen: production-like bursts; we typically see 60% of traffic in short windows.
[11:29] Arjun Patel: noted, we'll configure a burst profile and include both q4_0 and FP16 runs.
[11:36] Maya Chen: wrapping up — recap of next steps and action items, we'll share the scoring sheet, guardrail examples, and benchmark plan. arjun will own the benchmark config, maya will send pricing/estimate.
[11:53] Sara Lopez: thanks everyone, appreciate it. we'll upload extra prompts and confirm success criteria by Friday.
[12:05] Tom Nguyen: bye all.
